title: The natural numbers together with the rationals are two-universal for countable linear orders
source_title: Scott sentence complexities of linear orderings

proof_spans.label: the complete author proof of lem:universal, retained line for line

standard_prerequisites.name: Two-universality
standard_prerequisites.statement: A class K is two-universal for the class of linear orders when every countable linear order stands in the rank two back-and-forth relation to some member of K.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what the lemma establishes for N together with Q.

standard_prerequisites.name: Density of the rationals
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every interval of Q is infinite and has the order type of Q.
standard_prerequisites.use: It supplies the rank one comparisons used in the proof.

core_obligations: Split on whether the given countable linear order A is finite: a finite order already lies in the class (source lines 814-815).
For infinite A, note that every interval of Q is infinite and therefore stands in the rank one relation to any interval of A (source lines 815-817).

Read off A at most Q in the rank two relation from those interval comparisons, which gives two-universality of the class and, in particular, of the singleton of Q for infinite orders (source lines 817-818).

proof_roadmap.step: Finite case: the order is already a member.
Infinite case: compare intervals of Q with intervals of the order at rank one.
Assemble the rank two comparison and the two conclusions.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source0.tex lines 809-812: the class consisting of the natural numbers and the rationals is two-universal for all countable linear orders, and in particular the rationals alone are two-universal for the infinite ones. The statement gives no witness and no rank bookkeeping, and the proof (source lines 813-818) has to supply both: it separates the finite orders, which are already members, from the infinite ones, for which the comparison at rank two has to be produced through a rank one comparison of intervals, using that every interval of the rationals is infinite while an interval of an arbitrary countable order need not be. The reduction of a rank two comparison to a single interval comparison is the whole argument and it is invisible in the statement.
